name: Eskimo-Aleut Family

formality.description: Eskimo-Aleut languages express formality through kinship-based address and discourse style rather than pronominal T-V distinctions. Respectful language for elders and ceremonial contexts uses specific discourse markers, vocabulary, and indirect speech patterns.

gender.inclusiveGuidance: Eskimo-Aleut languages have no grammatical gender. Pronouns do not distinguish gender. Third-person referents are tracked through demonstrative systems and switch-reference rather than gendered pronouns.

linguisticChallenges.extremePolysynthesis: Eskimo-Aleut languages are among the most polysynthetic languages in the world — a single word can encode what would be an entire sentence in English. Verbs carry subject, object, tense, aspect, mood, and multiple derivational morphemes. Inuktitut tusaatsiarunnanngittualuujunga ('I can't hear very well') is a single word. Word-level and even phrase-level MT is fundamentally inadequate.
linguisticChallenges.ergativity: Most Eskimo-Aleut languages use ergative-absolutive case alignment — the subject of a transitive verb is marked differently from both the subject of an intransitive verb and the object. This is the opposite of nominative-accusative systems (English, most European languages) and requires a fundamentally different approach to argument mapping.
linguisticChallenges.incorporatedMorphology: Noun incorporation is highly productive — nouns can be incorporated into verb stems to create complex predicates. This creates 'words' with no single-word equivalent in target languages. The incorporated noun is not a separate syntactic entity.
linguisticChallenges.dualNumber: Eskimo-Aleut languages distinguish singular, dual, and plural number — there are separate forms for 'two of something'. This three-way number distinction must be properly handled; most target languages only have singular/plural.
linguisticChallenges.demonstrativeSystems: Elaborate demonstrative systems distinguish referents by distance, visibility, position relative to speaker, and motion. Inuktitut has 30+ demonstrative roots. These fine-grained spatial distinctions have no equivalent in most target languages.
linguisticChallenges.dialectalVariation: Significant dialectal variation across communities, even within the same language. Written standardization is often contested or incomplete. Different communities may use Latin script, Canadian Syllabics (ᐃᓄᒃᑎᑐᑦ), or Cyrillic.

notes: Family card for Eskimo-Aleut (~14 members). Covers Inuit (Inuktitut, Inuinnaqtun, Kalaallisut, Iñupiaq), Yupik (Central Alaskan Yup'ik, Siberian Yupik), and Aleut. Promoted from genus-level to family-level card. Script is null because members use Latin, Canadian Syllabics (Unified Canadian Aboriginal Syllabics), and historically Cyrillic.

regions.region: Canada (Nunavut, NWT, northern Quebec/Nunavik, Labrador), USA (Alaska), Greenland, Russia (Chukotka)
